entry: Precious gemstone, a variety of the mineral [[Corundum|corundum]], consisting of aluminium oxide with trace amounts of iron, titanium, cobalt, and chromium. Blue is the best-known color, but sapphires also occur in yellow, purple, orange, green, and colorless forms. The name derives from the Latin *sapphirus* and the Greek *sappheiros*, the latter referring to [[Lapis lazuli|lapis lazuli]]. Red corundum is called [[Ruby|rubies]] rather than sapphire. Sapphire ranks 9 on the [[Mohs scale]], the third-hardest mineral after [[Diamond]]. Natural stones are cut and polished for jewelry, while synthetic crystals are created in laboratories for industrial or decorative purposes. Non-ornamental uses include infrared optical components, wristwatch crystals, and the insulating substrates of [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuits]] and blue LEDs.

Externally threaded [[Fastener|fastener]], tightened or released by [[Torque|torque]] applied to its head. The head usually has a slot or other feature for a tool such as a [[Screwdriver|screwdriver]] or [[Wrench|wrench]], and it is larger than the body, which keeps the screw from being driven deeper than its length. Most screws have right-hand threads, tightened clockwise; left-hand threads are used where counterclockwise torque would loosen a right-hand screw, as on the left pedal of a bicycle. The screw was one of the last simple machines to be invented. It first appeared in [[Mesopotamia]] during the Neo-Assyrian period, and the Greek mathematician [[Archytas]] described it. By the 1st century BC, wooden screws were used in presses for olive oil and grape juice across the Mediterranean world. Metal screws became common fasteners only after [[Machine tool|machine tools]] for [[Mass production|mass production]] developed toward the end of the 18th century.

Increase in the global average level of the sea, accelerating mainly because of human-caused [[Climate change|climate change]]. Between 1993 and 2018, melting ice sheets and glaciers accounted for 44% of the rise, and thermal expansion of water for 42%. Rising seas increase coastal flooding and [[Storm surge|storm surges]], and low-lying Caribbean and Pacific islands, including [[Atoll|atolls]], face the greatest near-term impact on human populations.

Class of globular, spiny marine [[Echinoderm|echinoderms]]. Sea urchins live on the seabed in all oceans, at depths from the [[Intertidal zone|intertidal zone]] to the deep sea, and are typically 3–10 cm across. Their bodies are protected by a spiny, hard shell called a test, and they move slowly on tube feet. They feed mainly on [[Algae|algae]], and without predators they can create urchin barrens, areas devoid of large algae. Their embryos are easy to observe, so sea urchins have been studied since the 19th century as [[Model organism|model organisms]] in developmental biology. The fossil record dates from the [[Ordovician]] period, some 450 million years ago, and fossil urchins have been used as protective [[Amulet|amulets]].

Extinct family of early dinosauriforms of the [[Triassic]] period. Fossils have been found in Europe, North America, South America, Africa, and India. Whether silesaurids are the sister group of [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]] or belong within Dinosauria is debated. Most species are known from fragmentary fossils. Early forms such as Lewisuchus were small carnivores, while later ones were specialized [[Herbivore|herbivores]].

Oil painting by the Italian artist [[Raphael]]. Commissioned in 1512 by [[Pope Julius II]] for the church of San Sisto in Piacenza, it was probably executed c. 1513–14 and is one of the last [[Madonna (art)|Madonnas]] painted by Raphael. [[Augustus III of Poland]] bought it in 1754, and it was moved to [[Dresden]], where it remains. After [[World War II]] it was relocated to [[Moscow]] for a decade before returning to Dresden.

Medical disorder disrupting a person's sleep patterns and quality, with effects on physical, mental, and emotional well-being. Sleep disorders are classified by the International Classification of Sleep Disorders into [[Insomnia|insomnia]] disorders, sleep-related breathing disorders, central disorders of hypersomnolence, [[Circadian rhythm|circadian rhythm]] sleep disorders, parasomnias, and sleep-related movement disorders. Insomnia, difficulty falling or staying asleep without an obvious cause, is the most common. [[Sleep apnea|Obstructive sleep apnea]] affects 10–20% of middle-aged and older adults and involves repeated breathing pauses during sleep. Other examples include [[Narcolepsy]], [[Sleepwalking]], and sleep disruption from teeth grinding ([[Bruxism|bruxism]]). Diagnosis commonly uses polysomnography and actigraphy, and treatment varies by disorder.

Set of regulations, [[Sanctions (law)|sanctions]], and mechanisms restricting individual behavior in line with [[Social norm|social norms]] and orders. Social control is considered one of the foundations of social order and is studied in [[Anthropology|anthropology]], criminology, law, political science, and [[Sociology|sociology]]. Informal control operates through the internalization of norms and values, a process called [[Socialization|socialization]], and includes shame, ridicule, sarcasm, and criticism. Formal control comprises external sanctions enforced by government to prevent chaos or [[Anomie|anomie]], which [[Émile Durkheim]] called regulation. The term was first introduced to sociology by [[Albion Woodbury Small]] and George Edgar Vincent in 1894, and in the 1930s it took on its more modern meaning of an individual's conversion to conformity.

2001 Japanese animated fantasy film written and directed by [[Hayao Miyazaki]]. Produced by Toshio Suzuki and animated by [[Studio Ghibli]], *Spirited Away* follows Chihiro Ogino, a ten-year-old girl who enters a world of [[Kami|kami]], or spirits of [[Shinto|Shinto]] folklore, after her parents are turned into pigs. She takes a job in a bathhouse run by the witch Yubaba to free her parents and herself. [[Toho]] distributed the film, which was released in Japan on July 20, 2001, and became the highest-grossing film in Japanese history with ¥31.68 billion, a record it held for 19 years. [[John Lasseter]], a [[Pixar]] animator, helped convince Walt Disney Studios to buy its North American distribution rights. It won the Golden Bear at the 2002 Berlin International Film Festival and became the first hand-drawn, non-English-language animated film to win the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, at the 75th Academy Awards.

American businessman, inventor, and investor. A pioneer of the personal computer, Jobs co-founded [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] with [[Steve Wozniak]] in 1976, and the [[Apple II]] became one of the first highly successful mass-produced microcomputers. After the board of directors fired him in 1985, he founded NeXT and bought the computer graphics division that became [[Pixar]], serving as its chairman until 2007. In 1979 he saw the commercial potential of the Xerox Alto, a mouse-driven computer with a [[Graphical user interface|graphical user interface]]. The [[Mac (computer)|Macintosh]], introduced in 1984, was the first mass-produced computer with a graphical user interface. Jobs returned to Apple as chief executive in 1997 after the company acquired NeXT, and he worked with British designer [[Jony Ive]] on the iMac, iPod, [[IPhone|iPhone]], and iPad. He resigned as chief executive in 2011.

Mathematical object defined as a family of [[Random variable|random variables]], often indexed by time. Stochastic processes model systems and phenomena that vary randomly, such as the growth of a bacterial population, an electrical current fluctuating from thermal noise, or the movement of a gas molecule. They have been applied widely in [[Finance|finance]], where seemingly random market changes motivated their use. Two classic examples are the [[Wiener process]], also called [[Brownian motion]], and the Poisson process. Louis Bachelier used the Wiener process to model price changes on the Paris Bourse. Categories include [[Random walk|random walks]], martingales, Markov processes, and Gaussian processes. The subject draws on [[Probability theory]] and on branches of analysis such as Fourier and functional analysis.

Biopsychological state of need for repeated consumption of a psychoactive substance, also known as drug dependence. Dependence is distinct from [[Addiction|drug addiction]], defined as compulsive drug use despite negative consequences. Withdrawal, the body's reaction to abstaining, promotes continued use through negative reinforcement, and it may involve physical symptoms, psychological symptoms, or both. The [[International Classification of Diseases]] classifies substance dependence as a mental and behavioral disorder. The DSM-5, released in 2013, replaced substance abuse and substance dependence with a single diagnosis of [[Substance use disorder|substance use disorders]]. Dependence potential varies by substance and individual, with dose, frequency, [[Pharmacokinetics|pharmacokinetics]], route of administration, and time as critical factors.

Horological device telling the time of day from the apparent position of the [[Sun|Sun]]. In its narrowest sense, it consists of a flat dial and a gnomon, whose [[Shadow|shadow]] aligns with hour-lines marked on the dial. The style must be parallel to the Earth's rotational axis to be accurate throughout the year, and its angle from horizontal equals the local [[Latitude|latitude]]. Sundials indicate local solar time, so corrections are needed for the equation of time, which can amount to 16 minutes, 33 seconds, and for longitude relative to the [[Time zone|time zone]]. The earliest known examples emerged in ancient Egypt around 1500 BCE. Sundials are valued as decorative objects and metaphors, though many inexpensive, mass-produced decorative sundials have incorrectly aligned gnomons and cannot be adjusted to tell the correct time.

Khmer emperor (r. 1113–1150). Posthumously named Paramavishnuloka, he is best known as the builder of [[Angkor Wat]], the largest Hindu temple in the world, which he dedicated to Vishnu and [[Shiva]]. He reunited the [[Khmer Empire]] and received tribute from vassals. He was enthroned in 1113 after maneuvering for power, and he sent a mission to the [[Chola dynasty]] of south India.His campaigns against the Chams were largely unsuccessful, though in 1145 he appears to have invaded [[Champa]], defeated its king, and sacked its capital. Historians rank him as one of the empire's greatest rulers, citing his monumental architecture, military campaigns, and restoration of strong government.

Ancient cross-cultural geometric symbol, used in Eurasia and in a few places in Africa and the Americas for thousands of years. It is a symbol of divinity and spirituality in [[Hinduism]], [[Buddhism]], and [[Jainism]], and in Hinduism the right-facing form symbolizes prosperity and good luck. In the Western world it was widely seen as a symbol of good luck until the 1930s. The German Nazi Party later adopted it as an emblem of the so-called [[Aryan race]], and it appeared on the flag of [[Nazi Germany]]. As a result of [[World War II]] and the Holocaust, Western societies strongly associate it with [[Nazism]], and displaying it is prohibited by law in several countries, with exceptions for religious symbolism. An early European text by [[Heinrich Schliemann]], published in 1871, reported more than 1,800 ancient instances from excavations at Hisarlik.

Country in West Asia, on the eastern Mediterranean coast in the Levant. Officially the Syrian Arab Republic, it has [[Damascus]] as its capital and largest city and a population of about 26 million. Syria was a French mandate until it gained de jure independence in 1945, and a 1963 coup by the military committee of the [[Ba'ath Party]] established a one-party state. [[Hafez al-Assad]] came to power in 1970, and his son Bashar succeeded him in 2000. The 2011 protests escalated into the [[Syrian civil war]], which displaced more than 6 million people. The [[Islamic State]] occupied roughly two-thirds of the country by May 2015 before its territorial defeat in 2017. Opposition offensives brought down the Assad regime on December 8, 2024, and [[Ahmed al-Sharaa]] was formally appointed president in January 2025. Syria is a founding member of the [[United Nations]] and the [[Arab League]].

Professional educator in a formal school or college setting. Teachers help [[Student|students]] acquire [[Knowledge|knowledge]], competence, or [[Virtue|virtue]] through teaching, and anyone may take on the role informally, as when showing a colleague how to perform a task. Their duties include preparing lessons according to agreed [[Curriculum|curricula]], giving lessons, and assessing pupil progress, and they have a legal duty to protect students from harm such as bullying and abuse. Teaching is shaped by social context, and the [[European Union]] has identified three broad areas of teacher competence: working with others, working with knowledge, technology, and information, and working in and with society. Scholarly consensus is emerging that required competences fall into knowledge, craft skills, and dispositions.

Oil-on-canvas painting by Dutch Post-Impressionist [[Vincent van Gogh]], painted in June 1889. It depicts the view from the east-facing window of Van Gogh's room at the asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, just before sunrise, with an imaginary village added. Van Gogh had voluntarily admitted himself to the asylum in May 1889, and he painted the work in a ground-floor studio. The celestial elements include [[Venus]] and the [[Moon]], although the Moon's depiction is not astronomically accurate. Scientific analysis confirms Van Gogh's use of [[Ultramarine|ultramarine]] and cobalt blue for the sky. The painting has been in the collection of the [[Museum of Modern Art]] in [[New York City]] since 1941, and it is regarded as one of the most recognizable paintings in the [[Western canon]]. Van Gogh himself called it a "failure" in letters to his brother Theo.

Theatrical culture of ancient Greece, centered on the city-state of [[Athens]]. The theatre was institutionalized there as part of the Dionysia, a festival honoring the god [[Dionysus]], and the three dramatic genres that emerged were tragedy, comedy, and the satyr play. Athens exported the festival to its colonies. [[Thespis]], the earliest recorded actor, is often called the inventor of tragedy, though his importance is disputed. The City Dionysia, with its tragedy competition, was created around 508 BC. The tragedians [[Aeschylus]], [[Sophocles]], and [[Euripides]] and the comic writer [[Aristophanes]] produced enduring works in the 5th century BC. Modern Western theatre draws on its technical terminology, its classification into genres, and many of its themes, stock characters, and plot elements.

British polymath and physician. Young is credited with establishing the wave theory of light of [[Christiaan Huygens]], in contrast to the corpuscular theory of [[Isaac Newton]], and his work was later supported by [[Augustin-Jean Fresnel]]. He was instrumental in deciphering the hieroglyphs of the [[Rosetta Stone]]. He formulated [[Young's modulus]], a measure of a material's stiffness, and proposed a trichromatic theory of color vision. He earned his medical degree at the [[University of Göttingen|University of Göttingen]], practiced medicine in London, and became physician to St George's Hospital in 1811. He also identified astigmatism as a distinct visual defect and served as foreign secretary of the [[Royal Society]] from 1802.

Tall, self-supporting structure, usually taller than its width. Towers are distinguished from buildings in that they are built to serve functions that use their height, such as the visibility of a clock or the defensive view from a [[Castle|castle]] tower, rather than to be habitable. They may also be built for observation, leisure, or telecommunication. The oldest known may be a circular stone tower in the walls of Neolithic Jericho, dating to 8000 BC. Ziggurats of Sumerian architecture, such as the [[Ziggurat of Ur]], were built in the 3rd millennium BC. Towers were used along the [[Great Wall of China]] during the [[Qin dynasty]] in 210 BC, and the [[Leaning Tower of Pisa]] was built from 1173 until 1372. Towers face limits from compressive loads, buckling, and wind-induced vibration, which can be addressed by tapering the structure or using tuned mass dampers.

Placement of a flexible plastic tube into the [[Trachea|trachea]] (windpipe) to maintain an open airway or to administer drugs. It is frequently performed on critically injured, ill, or anesthetized patients to facilitate mechanical ventilation. The most common route is orotracheal, with the tube passed through the mouth. A balloon cuff seals the airway, and the tube is connected to a [[Ventilator|ventilator]] or breathing circuit. Complications include dental injury, aspiration of stomach contents, and unrecognized placement in the [[Esophagus|esophagus]].

Italian semiotician, medievalist, and novelist. Eco is best known for the 1980 novel *[[The Name of the Rose]]*, a historical mystery combining [[Semiotics|semiotics]] with medieval studies and literary theory, and for *[[Foucault's Pendulum]]* (1988), which touches on the history of occultism. He wrote his thesis on the aesthetics of [[Thomas Aquinas]] and taught at the [[University of Bologna]] for much of his career. From 1985 he wrote a twice-monthly column, "La Bustina di Minerva," for the magazine *L'Espresso*. His output also included children's books and translations from French and English. His 1995 essay "Ur-Fascism" lists fourteen general properties that he believes comprise fascist ideologies.

Substance in the [[Gas|gas]] phase below its critical temperature. Water has a critical temperature of 374 °C (647 K), the highest temperature at which liquid water can exist. A vapor can be condensed to a liquid by increasing its pressure without lowering its temperature. When a vapor coexists with its liquid or solid form, the two are in equilibrium, and its partial pressure equals the [[Vapor pressure|equilibrium vapor pressure]] of that phase. Atmospheric water vapor condenses into droplets that form [[Fog|fog]] and [[Mist|mist]]. A vapor is different from an [[Aerosol|aerosol]], which is a suspension of tiny liquid or solid particles in a gas.

Chinese poet, painter, musician, and official of the [[Tang dynasty]]. Wang Wei is renowned for his nature poetry and landscape painting. About 400 of his poems survived, and 29 are included in the 18th-century anthology *Three Hundred Tang Poems*. No authenticated paintings survive, though later painting shows his influence, and no compositions for his music are preserved. He passed the palace examination in 721 with top place and held court posts, including in [[Chang'an]]. He hosted the poet [[Meng Haoran]] in 728, and later in life he became a devout Chan Buddhist and vegetarian. He spent ten years studying with Chan master Daoguang, and his poems were compiled at imperial command by his brother Wang Jin.
